name: Totontepec Mixe
variety: Mixe of Totontepec Villa de Morelos, Oaxaca (North Highland Mixe in the classification of Wichmann 1995; own name Ayöök)
sources: Crawford, John Chapman (1963). Totontepec Mixe Phonotagmemics. Norman: Summer Institute of Linguistics of the University of Oklahoma.
Schoenhals, Alvin & Schoenhals, Louise C. (1965). Vocabulario mixe de Totontepec. México: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano.
Wichmann, Søren (1995). The Relationship among the Mixe-Zoquean Languages of Mexico. Salt Lake City: University of Utah Press.
Suslak, Daniel F. (2003). The story of ö: orthography and cultural politics in the Mixe highlands. Pragmatics 13(4), 551-563.

Martínez García, Nereida Crystabel (2010). La contribución del análisis lingüístico en el desarrollo de sistemas de escritura: el caso del mixe de Santa María Yacochi. MA thesis, Universidad de Sonora. (Summarises Crawford's analysis of Totontepec.)
Jany, Carmen (2007). Phonemic versus phonetic correlates of vowel length in Chuxnabán Mixe. Proceedings of the 33rd Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society.
Jany, Carmen (2011). The phonetics and phonology of Chuxnabán Mixe. Linguistic Discovery 9(1).
Jany, Carmen (2014). The stability of word stress across Mixean languages. Linguistic Society of America Annual Meeting Extended Abstracts.
Hoogshagen, Searle (1959). Three contrastive vowel lengths in Mixe. Zeitschrift für Phonetik und allgemeine Sprachwissenschaft 12, 111-115.
Ladefoged, Peter & Maddieson, Ian (1996). The Sounds of the World's Languages. Oxford: Blackwell.
contrasts: nine vowel qualities, the largest inventory among the Mixe varieties: the six inherited vowels i e a ɨ o u and three innovations written ä, ë and ö

eight kinds of syllable nucleus for each vowel (Crawford 1963): short V, long Vː, short checked Vʔ, long checked Vːʔ, rearticulated VʔV, aspirated Vh, long aspirated Vːh and rearticulated aspirated VʔVh
modal versus glottalised (creaky or interrupted) versus aspirated (breathy) vowels
plain versus palatalised consonants throughout the inventory; palatalisation also carries grammatical meaning (third person and other prefixes)
no voicing contrast in obstruents; s, l, r only in loans and sound-symbolic words
allophony: /p t̪ k/ are voiced between vowels ([β] or [b], [d̪], [ɡ]); in Chuxnabán Mixe all obstruents, affricates and fricatives included, are voiced between vowels and after nasals and voiceless at the end of a word (Jany 2007)
word-final stops are released with aspiration (ayöök ends in [kʰ])
/β/ (written v) corresponds to the glide [w] of other Mixe varieties
palatalisation affects the neighbouring vowels, with a palatal on-glide and off-glide
words written with an initial vowel begin with a glottal stop, realised as creak on the first part of the vowel
breathiness occupies the last part of an aspirated vowel; glottalisation can fall on the end (Vʔ) or the middle (VʔV) of the vowel (described for Chuxnabán Mixe by Jany 2007)
syllable_structure: CVC with an obligatory onset, one of the eight nucleus types and a coda of one to three consonants; CV in affixes
phonotactics: every syllable has an onset; the glottal stop fills it in vowel-initial words
roots are mostly one heavy syllable; affixes and clitics add light syllables
codas of two and three consonants occur, as in the numerals two and four in the eSpeak NG word list (ending in jtsk and xk)
the length and phonation contrasts are carried by the root syllable

stress.type: fixed on the root; morphologically conditioned
stress.rule: Stress falls on the rightmost heavy syllable of the root, which is usually the only heavy syllable of the word; prefixes, suffixes and clitics are unstressed (Jany 2014 for the Mixean languages in general).
stress.cues: not measured for Totontepec; the stressed syllable is the one that carries the length and phonation contrasts

rhythm.vowel_reduction: not described in the sources consulted
rhythm.notes: No rhythm study exists to my knowledge; class and final lengthening are neutral defaults. In Chuxnabán Mixe vowels in open syllables and before the retroflex fricative are longer than elsewhere (Jany 2007).

length.notes: No duration measurements exist for Totontepec. For Chuxnabán Mixe, a different variety, Jany (2007) measured short vowels of about 0.14 to 0.24 s and long vowels of about 0.28 to 0.37 s in monosyllables in a carrier phrase, with a constant ratio across vowel qualities; checked Vʔ was longer than plain V, rearticulated VʔV shorter than plain long VV, and aspirated vowels longer than plain ones. A three-way length contrast is reported for Coatlán Mixe (Hoogshagen 1959) and was not confirmed for Chuxnabán; it is not established for Totontepec.

intonation.notes: The pitch range value is a neutral default.

tone.notes: Mixe languages have no lexical tone; the laryngeal contrasts are phonation types.

phonation: glottalised vowels: checked (Vʔ) and rearticulated or interrupted (VʔV), realised with creak or a glottal closure
aspirated vowels (Vh), realised with breathiness at the end of the vowel

problems: the glottal stop is never produced in running text: the saltillo letter U+A78C, for which the rule is written, is read aloud as the word 'saltillo'; the ASCII apostrophe and U+2019 are dropped with a pause; U+02BC is spelled out as a symbol. All glottalised nuclei (Vʔ, VʔV) are therefore lost
m, n and ŋ are defined as the syllabic nasals of the base table, so every nasal forms a syllable of its own and can take the stress (mäjk comes out with a stressed syllabic m)
long vowels written double are two vowel segments in two syllables (tuun has two syllables) instead of one long nucleus

the letter j, which spells /h/, triggers the palatalisation rules, so a consonant next to /h/ gets a palatal glide (töjtïk comes out with [tʲ]); the letter y, which spells the palatal element, is only [j]
ä is a back vowel [ɑ], where the descriptions have a front low vowel /æ/; ï is close-mid [ɘ] rather than close /ɨ/; ö is the diphthong [əʊ]
stress follows the engine default (penultimate syllable) instead of the root syllable
aspirated vowels are a vowel plus a full [h] segment, with no breathy voice on the vowel
Spanish is used for letter and symbol names
good: nine vowel letters are kept apart
voicing of p, t, k, ts and x between vowels and after nasals
aspirated release of word-final p, t, k

notes: The phonetic symbols for the three innovated vowels are uncertain. Crawford (1963), as summarised by Martínez García (2010), has a low front vowel, a mid central vowel and a mid back vowel besides i e a ɨ o u, with o itself low back; Martínez García writes the vowel of ayöök as [ɤː]; Suslak (2003) calls ö a diphthong; an orthography proposal cited by Martínez García equates ö and ü with front rounded vowels. The symbols æ, ə, ɤ used here follow the first two sources and should be checked against Crawford and the Schoenhals vocabulary before they are used for formant targets. The eSpeak NG orthography writes the central vowels as ï and ë.
